headline: Bullish on deeply unloved liquor retailer at 9–12x earnings; market has forgotten Dan Murphy's brand value despite serial underperformance since spin-off
reasoning: Endeavour has been a serial underperformer since being spun out roughly three years ago and has not had a good reporting season since then. However, Tim Hillier argues the valuation at 9–12x expected earnings is very undemanding and that the market has forgotten that its core Dan Murphy's brand was once very favourably viewed. The price more than compensates for the risk being taken on.
quote: Look, the probably the one of the companies that we use as an example of that is Endeavour. They are facing a very weak market for liquor retail at the moment. That is, that has been a serial underperformer since it was spun out of almost about 3 years ago. In fact, I don't think they've had a good reporting season since then. And yet again, it seems that the outlook remains very challenging for that business. I think the valuation today is very undermining. It's probably on the order of 9 to 12 times earnings that that we expect that business to make in in due course. And the markets team used to have forgotten that one of his core retail brands being Dan Murphy's used to be very favourably, favourably viewed by investors and at some point they might come to appreciate it again. We often find that when the outlook is challenging, the price more than compensates you for the risk that you are taking on and certainly in the case of something like Endeavour, we think there is not much priced into into the company today.

headline: Allan Gray's Tim Hillier is buying Dexus at a ~30% discount to external valuation and an implied cap rate of ~8.3%, well above historic norms.

Replacement cost including land, construction, development margin, taxes and tenant incentives runs to $20,000–$30,000/sqm in major CBDs, making the current implied price extremely attractive. The implied cap rate of ~8.3% is at the high end of the 30-year historical range of 5–9%, providing an attractive yield while investors wait for the supply/demand imbalance to correct. He views the portfolio quality as reasonably high, with much of it in prime CBD locations, which he considers important for long-term resilience.
quote: Today, for decades, you probably pay about $10,000 per meter squared as an investor in Dexus for what is a fairly attractive office portfolio, and that's significantly below what external valuers think that those assets are probably worth. They assess them at about $14,000 per meter squared. So an investor today can acquire those assets at a discount of about 30% to that valuation... an investor in Dexus today is paying an implied cap rate of about 8.3%. Um, and that's a rough measure of yield. To put that in context, cap rates have ranged from about 5% to 9% over the last 30 years. So it's definitely at the higher end of that. So you kind of pay to wait in some ways.
episode_title: High-rising opportunities in this office property stock

headline: Allan Gray Australia holds ~5% of Australian equity strategy in Dexus as a high-conviction office REIT play at major valuation dislocation
reasoning: Tim Hillier notes that Allan Gray has approximately 5% of its main Australian equity strategy allocated to office landlords, with Dexus being one of the two holdings. Allan Gray generally dislikes REITs due to poor cash flows, but takes positions when there is a major dislocation and extremely attractive pricing. The current environment mirrors 2020 when retail REITs were deeply out of favour and available at a 40% discount to NAV — today office REITs are similarly despised by the market. Hillier sees investor sentiment as a contrarian opportunity, expecting a potential re-rating as sentiment toward office improves over time.
quote: I think well, full disclosure, at the moment we have about a little bit over 5% of our main Australian equity strategy invested in office landlords, those being Dexys and Mirvac. Um, but we really don't like these office or sorry, REITs in general. Really estate investment trusts, they tend to have fairly poor cash flows. So it really takes a major dislocation, an extremely attractive price to make us look at allocating capital to the sector. Most recently, our previous investment in REITs was in 2020. At that time, it was the retail landlords that were rarely out of favour. Investors were concerned about the competition from online retail. And then of course, malls closed in Covid and we were able to acquire the retail REITs at a 40% discount to their asset value. So at that time, we were surprised that investors were so pessimistic about retail, but had a fairly favorable view on office. Today, it's the complete opposite. Investors are quite have quite a favourable view on retail. But they despise offers. We don't know when that will change, but at some stage investors may have a slightly more favourable view in office.
episode_title: High-rising opportunities in this office property stock

headline: Allan Gray's Tim Hillier sees compelling value in Australian office property despite sector headwinds, citing steep discounts to valuation and replacement cost.
reasoning: Hillier argues that Australian office is deeply challenged — vacancy around 20%, landlord incentives at ~40%, and effective rents below 2019 levels — but that this creates attractive entry prices for contrarian investors. He notes that construction costs have risen ~50% since 2019, making new office development uneconomic, which should eventually choke off supply and allow rents to recover. Investors today can acquire office assets at implied cap rates of ~8.3%, near the top of the 30-year historical range of 5–9%, meaning you are 'paid to wait'. The key risk is AI-driven workforce reduction compressing office demand, though he notes AI data centre construction may paradoxically absorb construction resources and further constrain new office supply pipelines.
quote: Office is extremely challenged at the moment. The fundamental problem is that too much supply has come to the market, just at a time when demand hasn't been there to absorb that extra supply... rents are probably lower than they were in 2019. As we've discussed, construction costs are probably 50% higher than they were back in 2019 today. So there's a complete disconnect at the moment. And as a result of that, it makes no sense to develop office today. And we are seeing pipelines for new office supply drying up completely... in time we think a lack of supply will see rents increase. Uh, very hard to know exactly when that plays out. But today's lower prices mean that investors get a higher yield than they used to get.
